While the prelims set the tone early, Saturday’s main card elevated things to another level, capped by a fast-paced main event to close things out.
Tina Black kicked off the action by winning the Ultimate Fighter 34 strawweight tournament with a second-round stoppage win over Melissa Amaya before the bantamweight finale between Ilimbek Akylbek and Mahammadali Osmanli ended with Osmanli getting disqualified for an illegal knee. Recent Dana White’s Contender Series grad Luis Hernandez followed with a short-notice, 57-second submission win over Sedriques Dumas, followed by Ailin Perez extending her winning streak to seven by edging out Norma Dumont.
And in the main event, Raul Rosas Jr. and Raoni Barcelos got after it for four rounds, with Rosas Jr. coming away with a fifth-round stoppage win.
If you missed any of the action, get caught up with our recaps below.
More Coverage: Prelim Results | Scorecards
Raul Rosas Jr. rallied to secure a fifth-round stoppage win over Raoni Barcelos, earning a victory in his first UFC main event and sixth consecutive victory overall.
The 21-year-old Rosas Jr. came out of the gates quickly, peppering Barcelos and getting out to an early lead with significantly improved striking. But the Brazilian had moments of his own in the opening stanza and slowly started to creep ahead a little more with each successive round, leaning on his experience and savvy to pull away from the young phenom.
In the fifth round, Rosas Jr. came out looking to take the fight to the veteran, with the two continuing to go hard to start the final frame. A little over a minute into the round, Rosas Jr. toppled Barcelos to the canvas with a thud and the Brazilian went limp, with Rosas Jr. quickly recognizing his distress and signaling to the referee to stop the fight.
While not the conclusion anyone wanted after such an outstanding fight, this was the statement effort everyone wanted to see from Rosas Jr., who stood his ground throughout and came out aggressively in the final round. This was a huge step up in competition and he passed the test, putting him in a position to continue climbing the divisional ladder.
Despite all the tension between them and the high stakes on the line, the fight between Ailin Perez and Norma Dumont wasn’t as spirited and eventful as anyone would have liked, with Perez earning a somewhat suprising unanimous decision win.
Perez was able to take the Brazilian down in the opening round but failed to do anything of significance with the position, largely grinding out time and keeping Dumont pinned to the canvas. Dumont drew level by scoring a takedown of her own early in the second before getting the better of the striking exchanges once they worked back to their feet, with the third playing out in similar fashion, minus the early takedown.
The judges were called upon to determine the winner and all three saw it the same, awarding Perez the win. Surprising decision or not, that’s now seven straight wins for the Argentinian, who continues to be a lightning rod in the division, and again called for a championship opportunity.
Luis Hernandez scored a first-round submission win on twodays’ notice to earn his first UFC victory, tapping out Sedriques Dumas in a flash.
The first left hand Hernandez threw landed and gave him the opportunity to close the distance and initiate the clinch. After spilling to the canvas, Hernandez attacked the choke as they wrestled up, adjusting his grip and execution to collect the tap.
Less than two weeks after earning his contract, Hernandez became the third member of the DWCS Class of ’26 to earn a stoppage win in their debut, joining Episode 1 standouts Anthony Wint and Bilal Hasan. “The Stache” has heaps of personality, but skills to back it up as well, as he’s now 8-0 with a 100 percent finishing rate with a bright future inside the Octagon.
Saturday’s Ultimate Fighter bantamweight finale ended prematurely, as Mahammadali Osmanli landed a blatant illegal knee while Ilimbek Akylbek was down, resulting in a disqualification win for Akylbek when the fighter from Kyrgyzstan was unable to continue.
Moments after the two men worked back to the feet following a brief grappling entanglement on the canvas, Akylbek slipped and fell to his knees, prompting Osmanli to charge forward and connect with a full force knee to the head while his opponent was still clearly down. The fight was immediately paused, Akylbek was down on the canvas and dazed for a few moments, and the fight was ultimately waved off.
Osmanli was disqualified and Akylbek was declared the winner, becoming the first fighter from Kyrgyzstan to win The Ultimate Fighter and the first to win by disqualification. Not the way anyone wanted things to end, but it was the right decision, and chances are we will see these two run it back sometime in the not-too-distant future.
Tina Black became the first Brazilian woman to win The Ultimate Fighter, claiming the mantle with a second-round stoppage win over Melissa Amaya .
The experienced veteran was far and away the more effective striker of the two throughout, showcasing precision and power in hurting Amaya multiple times in the first. After rushing in and getting clipped in return during the closing moments of the first, Black was far more patient in the second after stinging Amaya, picking her shots and putting her away.
Black, who competed on Season 5 of Dana White’s Contender Series before claiming titles in Invicta FC and A1 Combat, was the top strawweight pick of the season and showed why here. This was a poised and professional effort from Black, who finally can call herself a UFC fighter.

articles.title_orig: No. 21 Florida serves notice to the rest of the SEC with its takedown of No. 4 Ole Miss
articles.title_zh: No. 21 Florida serves notice to the rest of the SEC with its takedown of No. 4 Ole Miss
articles.content_orig:
Last December, Florida athletic director Scott Stricklin did more than just kick the proverbial Lane Kiffin tires.
But when it was clear that he'd be headed to Baton Rouge, Stricklin turned to, at that point, a little-known former Kentucky linebacker who'd led Troy and Tulane to successful seasons. Nine months later, Jon Sumrall's Gators are the toast of college football after a drubbing of the Ole Miss Rebels on Saturday . Florida's ability to control the line of scrimmage and move the ball on the ground may present serious problems for the rest of the league.
Despite a 24-point win over a top-five team Saturday, Sumrall quipped to reporters afterward, "We have not arrived."
No, Jon, you have. Florida vaults into our Top 10 at No. 3.
Plenty other wildness transpired on the fourth full Saturday of college football. In the Big Ten, for instance, Iowa (over Michigan) and Wisconsin (over Penn State) picked up comeback wins on the road, and Oregon gashed through USC's defense even without starting quarterback Dante Moore . In the SEC, the Longhorns remain our top-ranked squad after beating Tennessee, Alabama QB Keelon Russell seems like the real deal and OU's Brent Venables owes the Sooners back that contract extension. If you're wondering why more than half of our Top 10 is from the SEC, look at the non-conference power league records (the SEC was the only power conference with a winning record — 10-2 — against the others over the first three weeks).
Florida quarterback Aaron Philo had plenty reason to celebrate after the Gators' blowout win over Ole Miss on Saturday. (Matt Pendleton-Imagn Images)
In the Big 12, Utah cracked our Top 10. In fact, are the Utes the best of the Big 12? They've certainly played the toughest schedule yet of the challengers in the conference. With a win at Louisville, Wake Forest made it more difficult to answer a vexing question: Who the heck will challenge Miami in the ACC?
Let's hit the rankings, which, no, don't yet include Indiana (wins over North Texas, Howard, Western Kentucky and Northwestern don't get you ranked).
This week: beat Tennessee 20-17
No program in the country has the combination of two wins like Texas: Ohio State and at Tennessee. The Longhorns tried to cough it up late in Neyland Stadium, but they hung on to give QB Arch Manning a win at a special place (he wears jersey No. 16 because of uncle Peyton 's years in Knoxville). In an odd stat, Arch was sacked more times (6) than he threw incompletions (five). His 18-yard, third-down strike to Ryan Wingo on Texas' eight-play, 60-yard touchdown drive helped Steve Sarkisian's guys take a 10-point lead.
This week: beat Illinois 42-19
Last week, the Heisman Trophy seemed destined to head to Oxford and into the hands of QB Trinidad Chambliss. This week, it feels like it's right back to where it was originally: in Columbus in the glue-coated hands of Jeremiah Smith. The Buckeyes receiver and future NFL top-10 pick continued a heater of a season with 217 yards, 12 catches and four touchdowns on Saturday. He's up to more than 600 yards through four games and seven scores. He's a magician with his hands, catching nearly everything within a 2-mile radius.
This week: beat Ole Miss 52-28
Shocked? Don't be. The Gators have two wins in very impressive ways, scoring 44 points in a win at Auburn and then 52 against Ole Miss in The Swamp. First-year coach Jon Sumrall's team plays a physical brand of football that's fun to watch. They've rushed for nearly 550 yards in consecutive SEC games. That's no easy task. QB Aaron Philo is playing smart, consistent football and the Gators look like legit contenders in the league.
This week: beat Central Michigan 52-3
QB Darian Mensah's numbers through his first four games are simply absurd. Get this: He's got 12 incompletions — twelve! — and 14 touchdowns. Don't ignore that he's thrown for at least 330 yards twice, too. His favorite target, Malachi Toney (Baby Jesus!) caught another six passes for 120 yards on Saturday. The Hurricanes are as explosive as they've been the last few years. Can they continue the onslaught against a Clemson team that's, sort of, found some momentum?
Alabama QB Keelon Russell put on a show Saturday with four passing touchdowns and a rushing touchdown in a blowout win over South Carolina. (David Leong-Imagn Images)
This week: beat South Carolina 49-18
Next week: at Mississippi State
Perhaps it's time to start talking about QB Keelon Russell in relation to the Heisman Trophy, no? He's completing more than 70 percent of his passes, has eight touchdowns and two picks. On Saturday against the Gamecocks, Russell misfired on just six passes and threw four touchdowns. He's got plenty of pieces around him too. Kane Wommack's defense held South Carolina to a 21 percent clip on third downs.
This week: lost to Florida 52-28
The Rebels need the bye next week. After an emotional victory against former coach Lane Kiffin and LSU, they laid the egg in Gainesville without star running back Kewan Lacy. The Gators' defense swallowed Ole Miss' ground attack and pressured Trinidad Chambliss just enough. But the most concerning thing for Pete Golding is his defense, which was exploited earlier this year against Louisville, nearly collapsed in the second half against LSU and allowed almost 500 yards on Saturday.
This week: beat Purdue 49-10
Next week: at North Carolina
The Irish's schedule isn't glamorous so far. In fact, they haven't beaten a team that will finish ranked inside the top 25 at the end of the season (at least that's our assumption about Wisconsin, Rice, Michigan State and Purdue). But the wins are fairly dominant and despite the struggles at times to run the football, Marcus Freeman's defense is one salty group. They entered third in the country in total D — a ranking that won't move much after Purdue's 218 yards.
This week: beat Oklahoma 41-13
The Bulldogs haven't played the toughest schedule so far, which is why they're at No. 8. But between QB Gunner Stockton and Kirby Smart's defense, they appear to be legitimate SEC title contenders — again. On Saturday, they forced the Sooners into a plethora of mistakes, including two fumbles, an interception and a turnover on downs. It's no fun playing against the Dawgs defense, despite NIL and the portal making it more difficult for them to stockpile front-seven depth.
This week: beat Missouri 31-24
Get ready to hear a whole lot about a Mississippi kid named Kamario Taylor, the Bulldogs' electric sophomore starting quarterback. He's slung 14 touchdowns and just two picks and, most recently on Saturday, put up 360 yards passing against Missouri in State's first top-25 win in more than a decade. Are the Bulldogs perfect? No. The defense can be exploited but former head coach Zach Arnett, the defensive coordinator, has the unit playing good enough.
This week: beat Iowa State 31-17
Welcome to the Top 10, Utes! They nearly let a 17-point lead slip away, but QB Devon Dampier showed just how slippery he can be. Most folks thought Dampier might follow Kyle Whittingham to Ann Arbor. Not so fast! He stuck around with new coach Morgan Scalley, who's got Utah playing its always-dependable D. On Saturday, RB Wayshawn Parker had a breakout performance (18 carries for 174 yards and three total TDs).

The UFC Fight Night 289 main event was wild, fun, but also scary.
Raul Rosas Jr. continued his climb up the UFC bantamweight rankings, defeating veteran Raoni Barcelos in a thrilling war. The bout was ruled a knockout in Round 5, but it wasn't your traditional finish.
Rosas Jr. (13-1 MMA, 7-1 UFC) took down the Brazilian by the cage, and Barcelos (22-6 MMA, 11-5 UFC) almost immediately stiffened up and looked to be unconscious. Rosas Jr. noticed there was little resistance from his opponent, stopped himself from adding more damage on the ground, and stood up in victory.
Unfortunately, Barcelos remained on the ground unconscious. He was carried out on a stretcher and immediately taken to a nearby hospital in Las Vegas. There has yet to be an official medical update on Barcelos at the time of this writing, but there's a report that Barcelos is conscious .

articles.title_orig: Trump Promotes Criticism of Republican Who Broke With Him on Immigration
articles.title_zh: Trump Promotes Criticism of Republican Who Broke With Him on Immigration
articles.content_orig:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Florida, has made waves by publicly breaking with President Donald Trump over immigration.
"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says in a new campaign ad . "The same Hispanics that helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
In 2024, voters broadly trusted Republicans to handle illegal immigration. Through incompetence and cruelty, the Trump administration has lost that goodwill. The last election showed Republicans have a path forward on immigration. But to take it, they need to ditch the cruel memes and aggressive tactics that have plagued Trump's second term.
Salazar is right: Hispanics were a major part of Trump's 2024 victory. According to Pew Research Center, the president nearly tied former Vice President Kamala Harris among Hispanic voters, a group former President Joe Biden won by 25 percentage points in 2020.
Since then, Trump's gains among Hispanics have evaporated. In February 2025, according to Pew , 93% of Hispanics who voted for Trump approved of the job he was doing. By April of this year, just 66% did. Over the same stretch, his approval among all Hispanic adults fell from 36% to 22%, while among non-Hispanic adults, it slipped from 49% to 37%.
The drop in support can be attributed largely to the administration's mishandling of immigration.
The loudest headlines came out of Operation Metro Surge, the enforcement campaign that flooded Minneapolis with more than 3,000 federal agents last winter. The surge was driven more by political optics than by any strategic need, and it ended with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents shooting and killing two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
Worse yet, administration officials then smeared Pretti . White House advisor Stephen Miller called him a "domestic terrorist," and the Department of Homeland Security claimed he "wanted to do maximum damage and massacre law enforcement." Bystander video showed he never drew his holstered pistol, which he was licensed to carry. Americans noticed: 61% of voters told Quinnipiac University pollsters that the administration had not given an honest account of the shooting.
Previously: We need to change the way we talk about the ICE shooting | Opinion
By mid-February, Americans opposed ICE's tactics 62% to 31%, according to an ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll. The backlash presumably helped cost Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem her job.
Since Noem's firing, ICE has largely faded from the headlines, as DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin has worked to keep the agency out of the spotlight. That changed Sept. 20, when an ICE officer in Austin shot and wounded Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, a Venezuelan man with a deportation order who had fled a vehicle stop. The facts are still unclear, and there is no ICE body-camera footage of the shooting. After Minneapolis, Americans have little reason to give the administration the benefit of the doubt.

Beyond the heated environment it needlessly created in Minnesota, the administration has driven support away with its messaging.
Throughout Trump's second term, official government social media accounts have churned out memes , many of them about immigration. The White House posted a Studio Ghibli-style cartoon of a convicted drug trafficker weeping as she was arrested and has promised that "the memes will continue." Other posts have included mock travel ads for deportation flights, and the administration has co-opted endless TikTok memes and audio trends to celebrate deportations.
All of it undercuts the administration's posture on such a serious matter. Nobody has ever been won over to a policy by a cartoon of a crying deportee, criminal or not. All it does is deepen the divide.
Austin ICE shooting proves we've lost ability to wait for facts | Opinion
Frustration with Democrats' failures at the border handed Republicans an opening in 2024. Voters trusted Trump over Harris on immigration 51% to 38%. Republicans have since squandered that advantage, but the path to a sensible immigration policy isn't closed.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and injured a man in North Austin on Sept. 20, officials say.
The man who was injured in the shooting was identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, by Austin immigration lawyer Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who said she was hired to represent him.
The incident was followed by a swift reaction from elected officials, as the public protested the latest shooting involving federal officers in the United States this year.

Americans still draw a line between securing the border and Trump's broader crackdown. In a New York Times/Siena College poll in January, roughly half of voters approved of his handling of the border, while they were split on deportations and a clear majority said ICE had "gone too far." That gap shows sensible border policy still has broad support, despite the administration's spectacle of mismanagement and cruelty.
Trump's inroads with Hispanic voters in 2024 were thought to signal a new Republican coalition, and they showed that these voters could back a more conservative immigration policy. Those gains have all but vanished. What looked like a lasting Republican asset has become a serious liability heading into the midterms.
To win back their advantage on immigration, Republicans need to ditch the cruelty. The memes, ICE's aggressive tactics and the general callousness have soured Americans on policies that should command popular support for years to come.
Lawmakers like Salazar may be breaking with Trump for electoral reasons. But if they win in November, they will be the ones building the Republican Party's next approach to immigration. That approach should press Democrats on their weaknesses on the issue, without the cruelty that has defined Trump's second term.
